uncited: It differs from sibling methods like [Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement](958-volumetric-isosurface-rendering-with-intersection-refinement.md) by avoiding per-pixel ray traversal in favor of hardware-accelerated primitive rasterization, and from [Multiple Flat Shaded Opaque Isosurfaces](1498-multiple-flat-shaded-opaque-isosurfaces.md) by potentially using stencil logic for visibility rather than texture-encoded ordering.
The family shares a core mechanism: for each pixel, a ray is constructed from the camera through the pixel center into the volume domain.
Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts [S3, unofficial][S6, unofficial].

The final color is computed using local lighting models (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface [S3, unofficial][S5, unofficial].

The Upson-Keller method originated in the early days of 3D graphics when fixed-function hardware lacked programmable shaders, necessitating clever use of stencil buffers and alpha testing for isosurface extraction [2041-upson-keller-polygon-method.md].

The use of point primitives for isosurfaces emerged as a way to avoid the computational cost of generating and sorting polygonal meshes (like Marching Cubes) for dynamic data [8433-opengl-point-rendering-for-isosurfaces.md].
